tldr: This paper introduces PredVLA, an ultra-compact model with no robot-data pretraining and only 680,000 (0.68M) trainable parameters, demonstrating that sensorimotor modeling via predictive coding provides a powerful inductive bias that makes exceptionally effective use of a limited parameter budget.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of PredVLA. It consists of a frozen multimodal front end and a hierarchical predictive-coding recurrent controller (blue region, 0.68M parameters). Sensory observations (red) are not fed forward directly into the recurrent dynamics; instead, they update internal states exclusively via online latent inference driven by prediction errors (dashed line).
overview:
In recent years, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved great success in robot manipulation. However, with billions of parameters, they are massive, resulting in very high computational and deployment costs. While some studies explore lightweight alternatives, most remain at the hundreds-of-millions parameter scale and merely compress the prevailing "direct observation-to-action mapping" paradigm.

Taking a different view, the authors asked: rather than directly mapping observations to actions, could "predictive coding"—which predicts sensorimotor dynamics and uses prediction errors to correct internal states—be the optimal learning principle for compact models?

The developed "PredVLA" combines frozen general-purpose image and language feature extractors with a hierarchical recurrent neural network of only 680,000 (0.68M) parameters. It undergoes no pretraining on robot data. Sensory observations (visual features and proprioception) are never directly fed into the network's forward dynamics; they influence internal states solely through online latent inference via deterministic free-energy minimization (minimizing prediction error).

Evaluated on the LIBERO benchmark, PredVLA achieves an 86.9% mean success rate across the three short-horizon suites and 75.4% across all four suites. Under a controlled comparison against parameter-matched Transformer and LSTM behavior-cloning (BC) baselines, it achieves striking 3.7x and 7.4x performance advantages, respectively. A mechanism-by-mechanism ladder analysis reveals that approximately 70% of this performance gap stems from replacing the direct observation input pathway with the predictive pathway, demonstrating that predictive sensorimotor modeling serves as an exceptionally strong inductive bias for compact controllers.
contributions: Proposed PredVLA, a language-conditioned predictive-coding policy with no robot-data pretraining and only 0.68M trainable parameters that achieves high accuracy on the LIBERO benchmark (86.9% across three short-horizon suites, 75.4% across all four suites).
Demonstrated 3.7x and 7.4x higher success rates compared to parameter-matched Transformer and LSTM behavior-cloning baselines under the same frozen front end, action decoder, and evaluation protocol.

Designed a step-by-step ladder transition from PredVLA to a BC-RNN baseline, identifying that replacing the predictive pathway with direct observation inputs accounts for roughly 70% of the overall performance drop.
Enabled a strict separation between closed-loop and open-loop control by setting online inference iterations to 0, producing a completely open-loop policy without retraining or model modification.

sections.heading: Is shrinking massive VLAs the only way? A new predictive-coding approach
sections.summary: As VLA models have grown massive, compression efforts have largely remained at the scale of hundreds of millions of parameters. This paper asks whether sub-million-parameter policies can achieve high manipulation performance by utilizing predictive coding—sensor prediction and error correction—instead of direct observation-to-action mapping.
sections.details:
Large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models such as RT-2, OpenVLA, and $\pi_{0}$ have demonstrated impressive results in general robot manipulation. With success rates exceeding 95% on benchmarks like LIBERO, the effectiveness of large-scale pretraining has been firmly established.

However, these powerful systems contain billions of parameters and demand enormous computational resources. While compact models like TinyVLA and SmolVLA have emerged, they still operate at hundreds of millions of parameters, largely scaling down the prevailing paradigm of mapping observations directly to actions. This raises a fundamental question: to build a compact controller, must we simply shrink the same approach, or is there an alternative learning principle that can dramatically maximize a limited parameter budget?

The authors focused on "prediction" as an inductive bias. Instead of feeding observations directly into a policy to predict actions, they adopted predictive coding: the internal model generates and predicts sensorimotor dynamics, and prediction errors drive online latent state inference.

This led to "PredVLA." By pairing frozen general-purpose encoders with a hierarchical recurrent network of only 0.68M parameters, it keeps observations out of the direct feedforward path. In LIBERO evaluations, it outperforms parameter-matched Transformer and LSTM baselines by several times, validating the power of predictive modeling.

sections.heading: Where this work stands: efficient VLAs, test-time adaptation, and predictive models
sections.summary: Prior efficient VLAs still maintain hundreds of millions of parameters, whereas PredVLA operates at an entirely different scale of 0.68M. Unlike world models or test-time adaptation methods, its online inference modifies only latent state variables using prediction errors, leaving model weights untouched.
sections.details:
This work connects to four main areas:

- Efficient VLA policies
Research into lightweight VLAs is active, including SmolVLA (~450M) and Evo-1 (~0.77B), but these remain in the hundreds of millions of parameters. PredVLA, by contrast, uses only 0.68M trainable parameters in its controller. It clearly separates roles: frozen front ends handle general image and language representations, while a compact recurrent model learns only the task dynamics needed for manipulation.

- Test-time inference and adaptation
Methods like TTT-VLA, RoboTTT, and VLA-Corrector adapt prompts or weights at deployment time. PredVLA also optimizes at test time, but rather than updating model weights, it optimizes latent free variables predefined in the generative model. Keeping the model fixed, it infers latent states online to minimize error against observed data.

- Predictive and world-model-based policies
Predicting future observations is increasingly explored in approaches like GR-2 and video-prediction policies. However, most treat prediction as auxiliary features, auxiliary training tasks, or tools for planning, while current observations are still fed directly into the policy. PredVLA differs critically: sensory prediction error is the *only* input pathway through which new observations influence internal state.

- Predictive coding for sensorimotor control
Recurrent models rooted in the free-energy principle—such as PV-RNN, PC-RNN, and CERNet—have a long history of inferring latent states by minimizing prediction error, with demonstrations on physical robots. However, they had not been evaluated on standard language-conditioned VLA benchmarks like LIBERO, nor systematically compared with parameter-matched modern policies. PredVLA bridges this gap.

sections.heading: PredVLA's architecture: a hierarchical recurrent model without direct observation input
sections.summary: PredVLA combines a frozen front end with a hierarchical PC-RNN. Sensory observations are never fed directly into recurrent states; latent variables are updated exclusively through online error regression that minimizes free energy (prediction error plus a prior divergence penalty).
sections.details:
PredVLA's core architectural distinction is that sensory observations are not fed forward directly into the recurrent dynamics (see Figure F1). Observations appear solely in the free-energy objective, shaping latent states via prediction-error-driven inference.

3.1 Frozen front end
Language instructions are embedded using a pretrained sentence encoder (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) and compressed via fixed Principal Component Analysis (PCA) into a static vector $\mathbf{l}$. Visual observations from third-person and wrist cameras are independently encoded by an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18, compressed with fixed PCA, and concatenated. Proprioception (joint angles and gripper state) $\mathbf{q}$ is passed through directly. Neither image nor language encoders are pretrained on robot data.

3.2 Hierarchical dynamics
The recurrent core consists of four hierarchical modules (T, V, $\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{top}}$, $\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{bottom}}$). The shared top module T receives language and generates top-down priors for the visual branch V and action branch ($\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{top}}$, $\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{bottom}}$). Each layer has a characteristic timescale $\tau_l$ (16, 8, 5, 2 from T downwards), forming a temporal hierarchy where higher layers evolve slowly and lower layers evolve rapidly. Two lateral pathways exist: a bottleneck connection from visual state to upper action state, and an efference-copy connection routing action predictions back to the visual layer.

3.3 Free energy
Latent state inference minimizes a deterministic free energy $E$, defined as the sum of accuracy (squared prediction errors on vision and proprioception) and complexity (a quadratic penalty keeping posterior latent $c_q$ close to generative prior $c_p$).

3.4 Training
During training, posterior latents for each demonstration and timestep are treated as model parameters and jointly optimized with network weights via Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT). The loss combines free energy with action negative log-likelihood (NLL).

3.5 Inference via error regression
At test time (robot execution), network weights remain frozen. Across a sliding window of recent observations, latent variables $c_q$ are updated over $n_{\rm itr}=10$ gradient descent steps (error regression) to minimize free energy. Deterministic states are regenerated from these updated latents, and actions are output from $\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{bottom}}$.

A key property is "pure open-loop control": setting $n_{\rm itr}=0$ disables error regression entirely, leaving latents at their prior values as dynamics unfold forward. Because observations never enter, this extracts a strictly open-loop policy using identical weights and language conditioning without retraining.

captions.F1: Detailed architecture of PredVLA. Top language conditioning and bottom-left visual/proprioceptive processing are frozen. The central blue block is the 0.68M-parameter hierarchical recurrent controller, which predicts visual and action states and optimizes latent variables $c_q$ via backpropagating prediction errors (black dashed line) against actual observations.

sections.heading: Experimental setup: rigorous LIBERO comparisons at matched parameter budgets
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted across four LIBERO suites. PredVLA was compared against parameter-matched (~0.68M) Transformer and LSTM baselines, accompanied by a mechanism-by-mechanism ladder experiment stripping features down to a BC-RNN.
sections.details:
4.1 Benchmark and data
Evaluations used the four suites of the LIBERO benchmark: spatial, goal, object, and long. Each suite contains 10 tasks, with 50 official demonstration episodes per task. Models are trained and evaluated independently per suite.

4.2 & 4.3 Model, training, and inference setup
PredVLA has 675,732 (approx. 0.68M) trainable parameters. Timescales are expanded only for the long suite; the basic structure is otherwise identical. Test-time inference uses a 30-step sliding window and 10 error-regression iterations.

4.4 Evaluation protocol
Evaluations span 50 rollouts per task across 14 independent training seeds (500 rollouts per seed, 7,000 rollouts per suite).

4.5 Baselines
For fair comparison, Causal Transformer (BC-Transformer) and LSTM (BC-RNN) baselines were built using the exact same frozen front end, demonstration data, Gaussian mixture action head, and evaluation protocol, with trainable parameter counts matched within $\pm 5\%$ of PredVLA. Action-chunking Transformer variants (ACT-style, chunk sizes 8 and 16) were also included.

4.6 Mechanism ladder experiment
To dissect the architectural differences between PredVLA and a conventional BC-RNN, a 7-step ladder (L0 to L6) was designed, replacing one mechanism at a time:
- L0: Full PredVLA (with error regression)
- L1: No error regression ($n_{\rm itr}=0$, fully open-loop)
- L2: Latent free variables $c$ removed (pure predictive recurrent model)
- (L2b: Side branch adding direct image inputs to action layers of L2)
- L3: Predictive pathway removed; observations fed directly forward
- L4: All timescales unified to $\tau=1$ (temporal hierarchy removed)
- L5: Recurrent cells replaced with LSTMs
- L6: Independently implemented and trained baseline BC-RNN
This design precisely isolates which mechanism contributes most to performance.

sections.heading: Results: massive performance margins and the decisive role of prediction
sections.summary: PredVLA achieved 86.9% across the three short-horizon suites and 75.4% across all four suites, far outperforming parameter-matched baselines. The ladder experiment revealed that roughly 70% of the performance gap is lost the moment the predictive pathway is replaced with direct observation inputs.
sections.details:
5.1 Primary results and baseline comparisons
With only 0.68M parameters, PredVLA reached 83.2% on spatial, 88.4% on goal, 89.2% on object, and 40.6% on long. The three short-horizon suites averaged 86.94%, and the four-suite overall average was 75.35%.

Under matched conditions (Table 4), BC-Transformer averaged 19.73% across all suites, and BC-RNN reached 10.26%. On the three short-horizon suites, PredVLA outperformed the Transformer baseline by 3.7x and the RNN baseline by 7.4x. On an RTX 5090, control latency was 46 ms/step (21.6 Hz), running well within real-time limits. As shown in Figure F2, PredVLA approaches the performance of massive VLAs with hundreds of millions to billions of parameters (such as OpenVLA at 76.5% and Octo at 75.1%) using a fraction of the parameter budget.

5.2 Ladder experiment analysis: what drives success?
The ladder experiment (Table 5) revealed a striking pattern.
The largest single performance drop occurred between L2 and L3 (removing the predictive pathway in favor of direct observation inputs). The three-suite mean plummeted by 52.36 percentage points, from 63.92% to 11.56%. This single modification accounted for 70.4% of the entire performance gap between PredVLA and BC-RNN.
Adding direct visual inputs in side-branch L2b failed to restore performance (dropping to 48.60%), confirming that the gap was not simply a lack of access to visual features. Moving from L0 to L1 (disabling test-time inference) dropped performance by 8.83 points, and moving from L1 to L2 (removing training-time latent inference) dropped it an additional 13.34 points, indicating that the latent inference mechanism as a whole accounts for roughly 30% of the gain.

5.3 Ablation studies and sensory error channels
Removing the temporal hierarchy (unifying timescales $\tau$) caused a sharp 17 to 29 point drop on short-horizon suites. However, in non-predictive models (L3 to L4), setting timescales to 1 had negligible impact (-1.23 points), showing that temporal hierarchies deliver their value primarily when paired with predictive architectures.

Ablating visual versus proprioceptive error terms (Figure F4) and corrupting observations with noise (Figure F5) showed stark task-dependent differences. On the object suite, removing visual prediction errors caused minimal drop, whereas removing proprioceptive prediction errors caused a 14.17 point drop. The object suite was also exceptionally fragile to proprioceptive corruption. Accurately estimating the robot's own joint and end-effector states proved critical for object manipulation.

captions.F2: Trainable parameter count versus LIBERO success rate. PredVLA (red star) achieves a 75.35% success rate with only 0.68M parameters, rivaling existing large models (gray circles) possessing tens of millions to billions of parameters. In contrast, parameter-matched BC baselines (blue squares) exhibit substantially lower performance.
captions.F4: Change in per-task success rate when removing visual prediction errors (left) or proprioceptive prediction errors (right) during online inference. Red indicates performance drops, and blue indicates gains. While both modalities contribute similarly in spatial and goal, the object suite exhibits severe drops concentrated entirely around the removal of proprioceptive errors.
captions.F5: Impact of corrupting inference-window observations using data from different episodes. The horizontal axis $\alpha$ represents corruption ratio; dashed lines indicate open-loop performance. Policies remain relatively robust to visual corruption (blue), but proprioceptive corruption (orange) causes sharp degradation even at a 25% corruption rate.

sections.heading: Discussion: why predictive modeling succeeds in small-scale control
sections.summary: These findings highlight the value of changing the computational formulation of control rather than simply scaling model capacity. They provide deep insights into the synergy between temporal hierarchies and prediction, as well as task-specific sensory dependencies.
sections.details:
6.1 Prediction as an inductive bias for compact control
The core takeaway of this paper is not just that strong manipulation is possible under one million parameters, but that the predictive formulation is key to unlocking it. The poor performance of parameter-matched Transformers and LSTMs, alongside the 70% drop when swapping prediction for direct inputs, demonstrates how parameter-inefficient direct observation-to-action mapping can be under tight parameter budgets.
This does not invalidate large Transformer VLAs. However, for edge devices and constrained compute, reformulating control around predictive sensorimotor dynamics offers a far more effective path than simply distilling or compressing huge models.

6.2 Interplay of latent inference, online correction, and temporal hierarchy
Even with online error regression disabled (fully open-loop), PredVLA sustained success rates in the high 70s on short-horizon suites. This shows that the hierarchical recurrent dynamics learn smooth, coherent trajectories. Conversely, on the long suite where horizon lengths double, open-loop success fell steeply from 40.6% to 28.0%, showing that online error correction becomes indispensable as task horizons grow.
Furthermore, the finding that temporal hierarchies (multiple timescales) require predictive structures to be effective provides a compelling insight from cognitive science and neuroscience perspectives.

6.3 Asymmetry in sensory error channels
The observation that proprioceptive errors (joint and gripper states) impact policy success more heavily than visual errors has practical implications. Tracking the internal dynamics of how the robot's own arm moves, rather than continually recalibrating visual positions, proved essential for robust manipulation within a limited capacity.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook
sections.summary: PredVLA demonstrates strong performance on LIBERO with an ultra-compact 0.68M-parameter footprint, proving the efficacy of predictive coding. Future work points toward physical robot deployments and broader long-horizon multi-task control.
sections.details:
This paper presented PredVLA, a language-conditioned predictive-coding policy operating with only 0.68M trainable parameters and zero robot-data pretraining. On the LIBERO benchmark, it achieved an 86.94% mean success rate across three short-horizon suites and 75.35% across all four suites, substantially outperforming parameter-matched Transformer and LSTM baselines.

A systematic ladder analysis identified that the predictive-coding structure—specifically updating latent states via prediction error rather than feeding observations forward—drives roughly 70% of this performance gap. The study also provided detailed insights into latent inference, temporal hierarchies, and individual sensor channels.

Current limitations include evaluation restricted to simulation and a single robot morphology, training separate models per suite, and a modest 40.6% success rate on the long-horizon suite. Future directions include physical robot deployment, robustness against environmental disturbances, and extending toward unified multi-task learning within a single model.

takeaways: In sub-million-parameter robot controllers (<1M), sensor prediction and error regression (predictive coding) offer far greater parameter efficiency than direct observation-to-action mapping (behavior cloning).
Restricting observations from direct feedforward inputs and channeling them exclusively through prediction-error-driven latent updates accounts for approximately 70% of the performance margin.
Hierarchical timescales struggle in isolation but create a powerful synergistic effect when combined with predictive architectures.
Disabling online error regression yields a pure open-loop policy instantly, providing a clean method to isolate the true contribution of closed-loop feedback.
limitations: Evaluations are limited to simulation (LIBERO) on a single robot arm morphology, leaving robustness against real-world physical noise and disturbances untested.
Models are trained separately for each suite; multi-task generalization across diverse task suites using a single 0.68M model remains unproven.
Performance on the long suite remains at 40.57%, showing that trajectory drift and error accumulation over extended horizons remain challenging.
